How to use this package

Three ways to get value from it, depending on where you are right now.

Units used throughout Every temperature and size is given twice. Temperatures appear in degrees Fahrenheit (°F) with degrees Celsius (°C) beside them. Sizes appear in inches (in) and feet (ft), with centimeters (cm) beside them. Snakes and their food are weighed in grams (g), the unit a kitchen scale shows. Humidity is a percentage (%) of how much moisture the air could hold. Prices are in United States dollars.

If you haven't bought a hognose yet

Read the law section first, starting on page 22. In most states a western hognose raises no legal question at all, but in a handful it is banned, capped or permit-only, and in several more the answer depends on which of the three hognose species you buy. Then read pages 4 through 10 before buying any equipment. Two decisions are expensive to get wrong: the enclosure size on page 6, which depends on whether you buy a male or a female, and the heat source on page 8, which has to run through a thermostat, a controller that cuts the heat at a set temperature. The Budget and Shopping List on page 33 then lets you buy once instead of twice.

If your hognose is already home

Start by auditing what you have against the Setup Checklist in the print list below. Then read page 9: this species wants dry air, and an enclosure kept damp is the root of the two most common illnesses in it. If your snake hoods, hisses or rolls over to play dead, page 15 explains why that is normal. If it is refusing food, page 13 comes before any worry. If anything already looks wrong, go straight to Health Red Flags on page 25.

Print these first

Page 31: Setup Checklist & Targets
Page 32: Emergency & Quick Targets Card
Page 36: Symptom Quick Reference
Page 37: Daily, Weekly & Seasonal Routine
Page 39: Pet-Sitter Sheet
Page 40: Owner Log
Page 41: Equipment, Quarantine & Vet Log
Page 11: Prey Size & Feeding Schedule
Why this package exists The western hognose has a reputation built on two things: a theatrical defensive act, and the word "venomous." The act makes owners think a calm snake is an aggressive one, and the word makes owners think a mildly venomous snake is a dangerous one. Neither is true, and both are easier to live with once you know what is going on. The care itself is simple once three things are right: dry air, deep digging substrate (the loose material on the enclosure floor), and feeding an adult less often than a growing juvenile. Every figure here comes from veterinary and scientific sources, listed on page 45, and every temperature and dimension is given in both imperial and metric units.
Not a substitute for A veterinarian who sees reptiles. This is a husbandry reference for day-to-day care, and anything urgent is a professional call, not a page in this book. Find a reptile vet before you need one, and write the number on the emergency card. Nothing in the law section is legal advice either.

Section 01 · Profile

Quick profile

Everything at a glance before you read the detail.
Species coveredThe western hognose, Heterodon nasicus, also called the plains hognose. It is the hognose the pet trade sells. The eastern and southern hognoses are different species, and the difference matters for the law.
Native rangeThe North American plains, from southern Canada to northern Mexico: shortgrass prairie, dry rocky land, and sandy soil it can dig in
Adult sizeFemales run much larger than males. A typical adult male is 16 to 24 in (41 to 61 cm); a typical adult female 21 to 30 in (53 to 76 cm).
Captive lifespan10 to 15 years is the usual range, with 15 to 20 reported in captivity
ActivityActive by day, most of all in the morning and late afternoon, and a dedicated burrower
DietToads in the wild. In captivity, frozen-thawed mice, fed every 5 to 7 days while young and about every two weeks as an adult. Page 11
Enclosure, one adultMale: 20-gallon equivalent, about 30×13×13 in (76×33×33 cm). Female: 40-gallon equivalent, 36×18×16 in (91×46×41 cm). Floor space over height. Page 6
TemperatureBasking 90 to 95°F (32 to 35°C), cool side 70 to 75°F (21 to 24°C), nights at room temperature, no colder than 60°F (16°C). Page 7
Humidity30 to 50%: dry. One humid hide (a box or cave the snake can get inside) for shedding, and no misting the enclosure. Page 9
LightingA 12-hour day. UVB (ultraviolet B, the part of sunlight a reptile's skin uses to make vitamin D3) is not required, but a low-output tube suits this day-active snake.
Substrate3 to 6 in (8 to 15 cm) of loose, dry, diggable substrate, about 70% soil-based to 30% reptile-safe sand. Page 10
VenomRear-fanged and mildly venomous. Not considered dangerous to a healthy person. Page 16
Conservation statusLeast Concern, the lowest-risk category on the global Red List of threatened species, but listed as threatened in some states, Illinois among them. Buy captive-bred

Cost overview

Initial setup

The snake is $50 to $100 for a normal, wild-type animal (natural color and pattern), and far more for a rare color form. Females typically cost $50 to $200 more than males. Itemized, the equipment comes to $390 to $850, and the enclosure is the biggest single line. With the snake, a first exam and a fecal test (a stool check for parasites), plan on $505 to $1,080. Page 33 has every line.

Ongoing

Frozen mice, substrate, electricity, two UVB tubes a year if you run one, and a yearly wellness exam come to $235 to $390 a year, about $15 to $35 a month. A respiratory infection or an impaction can run into the hundreds to treat, and an X-ray image, called a radiograph, is $100 to $250 a view.

The number that should drive the decision Not the price. The lifespan. A hognose bought for a ten-year-old can still be in the house when that child leaves for college, and some live to 20. The purchase is the cheap part. The routine on page 37, and a reptile vet for every one of those years, is what you are signing up for.
Beastly FactsHognose Snake Care Package · Edition 1.14
Section 01 · Profile

Which hognose this is, size & lifespan

"Hognose" is a common name shared by several species. The law and the care both depend on which one you have.

Three hognose species live in the United States, and a fourth, the Mexican hognose, reaches into the southwest. The one sold as a pet is almost always the western hognose, Heterodon nasicus, which some state laws call the plains hog-nosed snake. Its smaller size, milder bluffing and flexible diet made it the hognose most keepers settled on, and most animals sold now are captive-bred rather than collected. This package is written for the western hognose only.

SpeciesWhere it fitsWhy it matters to you
Western (plains) hognose
Heterodon nasicus		The pet-trade species. Dry prairie and sandy groundEvery figure in this package. Several state laws name it directly, some to allow it and some to restrict it
Eastern hognose
Heterodon platirhinos		Native across much of the eastern half of the country. Its care differs: more humidity and a cooler basking spot than the westernProtected or restricted as a native species in many states that leave the western alone. Never collect one from the wild
Southern hognose
Heterodon simus		A southeastern nativeProtected by name in Alabama, and on Georgia's list of natives that may not be kept as pets
Get the species in writing State rules are written to the scientific name, and the common names overlap: "plains hognose" and "western hognose" are the same snake. Ask for a receipt that names Heterodon nasicus and says captive-bred. In several states that one line is the difference between a legal pet and a prohibited one. Pages 22 to 24.

How big, and how heavy

StageLengthWeight
Hatchling5.5 to 7 in (14 to 18 cm)Usually 4 to 7 g. Under 3 g happens, and 13 to 14 g is a record
Adult maleTypically 16 to 24 in (41 to 61 cm), many around 20 in (51 cm). Over 25 in (64 cm) is unusualSmall. Adult males are commonly fed as 40 to 70 g snakes
Adult femaleTypically 21 to 30 in (53 to 76 cm)150 to 200 g in a young adult, 220 to 400 g in an older one

Published ranges vary. Another range is 14 to 37 in (36 to 93 cm), averaging about 20 in (50 cm), at 80 to 350 g, and across the hognose species as a group the range runs 1.5 to 3.5 ft (45 to 107 cm). The weights in the table are a guide, not a target: your own snake's weight trend matters more.

How long it lives

10 to 15 years is the usual captive range, and 15 to 20 is reported in captivity. In the wild, a western hognose lives about 14 years on average, with a reported range of 9 to 19.

The animal behind the care

The upturned snout is a digging tool. The enlarged scale at its tip, the rostral scale, is shovel-shaped, and the snake uses it to burrow through loose soil after buried toads, its main wild prey. Toads can make up nearly 80% of the diet in some regions. In the wild it spends roughly September to March below ground. Every part of the captive setup follows from that life: dry air, deep loose substrate, and a snake that may slow down in winter.

Beastly FactsHognose Snake Care Package · Edition 1.15
Section 02 · Housing & Environment

The enclosure, sized by sex & age

A ground-dwelling burrower measures its home in floor space. Height does almost nothing for it.

The working rule is about one square foot of floor space per foot of snake length. Because females grow so much larger, the minimum depends on sex:

SnakeMinimum enclosure
Adult male20-gallon equivalent, about 30×13×13 in (76×33×33 cm)
Adult female40-gallon equivalent, 36×18×16 in (91×46×41 cm)
Either sex, a solid adult setupA front-opening enclosure of about 2×2×2 ft (61×61×61 cm), or 36×18×18 in (91×46×46 cm)
Hatchling under 6 in (15 cm)A 5-gallon enclosure, about 16×8×10 in (41×20×25 cm)
JuvenileA 10-gallon enclosure until it is about a year old. Starting in the adult enclosure also works, if it has enough hides and cover to feel secure

Front-opening PVC (polyvinyl chloride, a rigid plastic) or glass both work. If you use glass, cover three sides to cut stress. The lid has to latch: a hognose pushes at any gap it finds, and on a baby's enclosure the lid needs clamps or latches. Never use tape, which is notorious for injuring snakes. Keep one snake per enclosure: sharing an enclosure is one of the listed causes of regurgitation, a meal brought back up.

Where the enclosure goes

PlaceWhy
Out of the kitchenReptiles carry Salmonella bacteria with no sign of illness, and keeping the snake and its gear away from food is the first hygiene rule. Page 14
Out of a sunny windowThe thermostat controls the heat source, not the sun through the glass. Every degree should come from a controlled source, page 8
In a room you can keep steadyThe same heat source behaves very differently in a cold room and a warm one, so a stable room makes the gradient easy to hold
Beastly FactsHognose Snake Care Package · Edition 1.16
Section 02 · Housing & Environment

The temperature gradient

A hot spot at one end, a cool burrow at the other, and the snake chooses.
Zone°F°C
Basking surface, warm end90 to 9532 to 35
Middle of the enclosure75 to 8524 to 29
Cool side, where the deep substrate is70 to 7521 to 24
NightRoom temperatureRoom temperature
Add heat if the night falls below6016
A fault if the basking surface reads well above9535

At night the heat goes off and the enclosure can fall to room temperature, as long as it stays at 60°F (16°C) or above.

Why a gradient

A snake cannot make its own body heat. It sets its temperature by moving between warm and cool spots, so the enclosure exists to give it a choice. The hot spot is for digesting; the cool end is where this species digs, and where it goes to cool down. Where a reptile sits in its range has real consequences for how it fights infection, which is why a sick snake is kept toward the upper end of its normal range and why an enclosure should not run at the bottom of the range by default.

Reading it properly

  • Two digital probe thermometers, one probe on the basking surface and one on the cool end. One reading tells you nothing about a gradient.
  • An infrared thermometer, the handheld point-and-read kind, to spot-check the surface itself: the basking stone, the substrate, the wall near the heat. It finds a hot spot the fixed probes are not sitting on.
  • Check both before the snake goes in, and again whenever anything in the setup changes.

Night heat is a different setup

The basking light goes off at night, and a hognose needs no night bulb. A normal room is fine overnight as long as the enclosure stays at 60°F (16°C) or above. Only if your room drops below that, add a heat source that gives off no light, such as a heat mat or a ceramic heat emitter (a screw-in heater with no visible glow), on its own thermostat.

Signs the gradient is wrong

You noticeCheck
Wheezing, open-mouth breathing, mucusToo cool, too damp, or poor airflow are the causes of respiratory infection. Read every number, then call the vet. Page 26
A meal brought back upAn enclosure running too cool is one of the listed causes. Page 27
Basking surface well above 95°F (35°C)A fault, not a feature. Check the probe has not slipped and the thermostat works.
Two thermometers on the same spot disagree by more than a degree or twoOne has drifted. Replace it rather than averaging them
Beastly FactsHognose Snake Care Package · Edition 1.17
Section 02 · Housing & Environment

Heat sources, thermostats & probes

Whatever heats the enclosure, a thermostat controls it. That one device is what prevents burns.

The usual heat source for this species is a low-wattage halogen basking bulb (a bright, focused light bulb that heats the spot under it), mounted over the screen at the warm end and run on a dimming thermostat. A 50-watt halogen spot is a typical choice. Some keepers use an under-tank heat mat instead; the halogen is the better choice. Either way, the thermostat is not optional. Put a flat, light-colored stone or piece of wood under the lamp: wild hognoses bask on rocks and logs, and a flat surface warms the snake more efficiently.

Match the thermostat to the heat source

ThermostatHow it controls heatBest matched to
On/offCuts power fully at the set temperature, restores it when the reading dropsHeat mats, which change temperature slowly
Pulse proportionalSends short pulses of power for a steadier averageCeramic heat emitters, which can overshoot on an on/off cycle
DimmingTurns the power up and down like a light dimmerHalogen basking bulbs, with no visible flicker

These pairings are the usual best match, not a hard rule. What matters most is that the heat source has a controller at all.

Where the probe goes

A thermostat only regulates the spot its probe measures. For a heat mat, the probe goes on the floor of the warm hide, the surface the snake lies on, held with a probe clip or suction cup, never tape: foil tape over the probe throws off its reading, and a snake can stick to exposed adhesive and tear scales. For an overhead halogen, makers place the probe differently: on the basking surface under the lamp, or in the air a few inches below the bulb. Follow your own thermostat's instructions, keep the probe at the snake's level rather than up near the fixture, and confirm the result with the infrared thermometer.

Never without a thermostat, never within reach An unregulated mat or bulb keeps drawing full power with no ceiling, and a snake pressed against an overheated surface does not always move away in time. That is how a burn happens. Keep any overhead source at least 4 to 6 in (10 to 15 cm) above the highest spot the snake can reach, behind the screen. Skip heat rocks entirely: they burn snakes and heat poorly.

Plan for the thermostat failing

  • The probe slips. The most common failure, and a silent one: the display stays accurate for the wrong spot. Look at the probe at every water change.
  • The thermostat sticks on. Rarer and more dangerous. A second thermometer, away from the thermostat's probe and read daily, is what catches it.
  • Wattage is a starting guess. The number on the box assumes an average room. Set it up, then measure for a day before the snake goes in.
Beastly FactsHognose Snake Care Package · Edition 1.18
Section 02 · Housing & Environment

Dry air, the humid hide & ultraviolet light

The number that prevents the most illness in this species is a low one.

Keep ambient humidity at 30 to 50%, dry by the standard of most pet snakes. Do not mist the enclosure to raise it. Running the whole enclosure damp is a direct path to respiratory infection and scale rot, two illnesses that both trace back to the same cause. A western hognose comes from prairie and sandy ground, and that makes its setup drier than a ball python's or a corn snake's.

The one humid spot

Give the snake one humid hide for shedding: a hide whose substrate is mixed with a little water, or packed with moist sphagnum moss, while the rest of the enclosure stays dry. Add moisture there only as needed, mostly when a shed is coming (page 29). Set it between the warm and cool ends so the snake can use it at a comfortable temperature.

Measure it, don't guess it

A digital hygrometer (a humidity meter) is core equipment here, not an extra, because this species' whole setup depends on humidity being confirmed low rather than guessed at. Read it at snake level, away from the water dish and the humid hide.

A day and a night

Unlike most pet snakes, a hognose is active by day, so it gets a normal day and night: lights on a timer, 12 hours on and 12 off. An optional seasonal schedule runs longer days in summer and shorter ones in winter.

Ultraviolet light

UVB is not strictly required, and a hognose will not die without it. But a low-output UVB tube suits this day-active species. The specification that fits:

WhatSpecification
TubeA T5 HO tube (T5 is the slim fluorescent tube, 5/8 in across; HO means high output) sold as "5.0" or "6%" strength
Strength at the snakeUVI (ultraviolet index, a measure of UVB strength at one spot) peaking at 1.1 to 3.0 where the snake basks. Hognoses sit in Ferguson zone 2, the band for partial-sun and occasional baskers, about 0.7 to 1.0 across the gradient
LengthAbout two-thirds of the enclosure length: about 24 in (61 cm) for a 36 in (91 cm) enclosure, at the warm end
DistanceAbout 10 to 14 in (25 to 35 cm) from the tube to the snake's back on the basking surface, with the tube over the screen. Ordinary glass and most plastics block most UVB, so the tube never sits above a glass lid
Timer and replacementOn the same 12-hour timer as the light. Replace the tube on the maker's schedule, 6 to 12 months depending on the model and no longer than 12, even if it still lights up: UVB fades before the visible light does
MeterA UV index meter is the only way to know the tube is at the right height and when to replace it; UV cards show total UV, not the UVB that makes vitamin D3.
Deep substrate makes UVB safe A burrowing snake controls its own exposure: it basks when it wants and goes under the cool-end substrate when it has had enough. That is why the tube goes at the warm end and the digging goes at the cool end.
Beastly FactsHognose Snake Care Package · Edition 1.19
Section 02 · Housing & Environment

Deep bedding, digging & cleaning

For a burrower the substrate is not decoration. It is the part of the enclosure the snake lives in.

Provide 3 to 6 in (8 to 15 cm) of loose, dry, diggable substrate. A soil and sand mix works well: roughly 70% soil-based substrate to 30% reptile-safe sand is a common ratio, and aspen or coconut fiber works as the soil-based part. Depth is the variable that matters. Give the snake enough to disappear into completely, not just to push around, and choose a mix that holds a tunnel rather than collapsing. A depth a hognose can vanish into takes more than one small bag. Keep it dry: damp substrate plus this species' preference for arid conditions is a fast route to skin and respiratory problems.

Put the digging on the cool end In the preference study on page 17, western hognoses chose the enriched side more strongly when it was also the cooler side. So: deepest substrate at the cool end, basking surface at the warm end, cover at both. The snake never has to choose between the temperature it wants and the behavior it wants.

Furnishings

ItemWhy
Warm hide and cool hideTwo secure hides minimum, one at each end, so hiding never costs the snake its preferred temperature
Humid hideFor shedding.
Cork bark, branches, leaf litterBreak up the floor so there is cover everywhere, not only in two boxes
A large water dishBig enough for the snake to get into. It supports shedding and drinking and gives the snake an option it controls
Flat basking stoneUnder the lamp at the warm end. Page 8

Never feed on the substrate. Feed in a separate container, page 12: a hognose that takes a mouse with a mouthful of substrate attached is the impaction case on page 27.

Cleaning

WhenWhat
As you see itPull out droppings and urates (the white, chalky part of a reptile's waste)
DailyEmpty, wash and refill the water dish with fresh water
About every 3 monthsReplace the whole substrate even if it looks clean, because urine soaks into it, and disinfect every surface and hide while the enclosure is empty. This longer interval holds only for a bed kept dry with every dropping pulled the day it appears
Monthly insteadFor a bed that has gone damp, smells, or hid a dropping for days

A bioactive setup, a planted substrate with a cleanup crew of tiny invertebrates, is the exception and can run for years without a full change. To disinfect: scrub first, then household bleach at 1:32, which is half a cup per gallon of water, kept wet on the surface for 10 minutes, rinsed until no bleach smell remains, and aired for a full day before the snake goes back. Do it in a utility sink, a dedicated tub or outdoors, never the kitchen sink or a bathtub people use.

Beastly FactsHognose Snake Care Package · Edition 1.110
Section 03 · Feeding

Prey size & feeding schedule

A hatchling can weigh 3 g. At that size the question is not which mouse, but which part of one.

Mice are the staple and the best diet for this species, fed frozen-thawed: frozen, then thawed before feeding. Never live: a live rodent can injure a snake that does not subdue it at once, and a 3 g hatchling has no margin for that. Larger individuals sometimes take small rats. Gerbils, hamsters, multimammate mice and chicks are fallbacks for a snake that will take nothing else.

Prey size for hatchlings, by the snake's weight

The chart runs by weight, which is more useful than age for an animal that arrives at wildly different sizes. Weigh the snake on a kitchen scale in grams.

Snake weighsPrey
3 g and underA small pinky head. A pinky is a newborn, hairless mouse
4 to 6 gExtra small pinkies
7 to 9 gSmall to medium pinkies
Larger juvenilesLarge pinkies to peach fuzzies, then peach fuzzies to fuzzies. A fuzzy is a young mouse with its first fur; a peach fuzzy sits between

Past the hatchling stage, size prey by proportion: a prey item slightly thicker than the snake at its thickest point. A 70 g adult male may settle on a hopper (a young, weaned mouse) or a couple of fuzzies. A large adult female works up to considerably bigger prey.

How often

SnakeFeed every
Hatchlings and juveniles5 to 7 days, or simply weekly
Adult malesAbout every two weeks, the default for any adult. Metabolism slows with maturity
Mature females10 to 14 days; some large females 14 to 21
The most common feeding mistake with this species Keeping an adult on a hatchling's schedule. An adult fed weekly gets fat, and obesity is a real contributor to shortened lifespans in hognoses. Match the frequency and the portion to the adult's activity and size, not to the schedule that suited it as a fast-growing juvenile. Diets high in protein may also predispose a reptile to uric acid building up in the body, which can cause gout, a painful disease of the joints and organs.

Keep a feeding record

Write down every meal: the date, the prey, and whether it was taken. Weigh the snake once a week on the same scale. A hognose that is getting sick often shows it on the scale before it shows it anywhere else, and a feeding record is what turns "it seems off" into something a vet can use. The Owner Log on page 40 is set up for exactly this.

Beastly FactsHognose Snake Care Package · Edition 1.111
Section 03 · Feeding

Frozen prey: thawing, storage & where to feed

The part most keepers get sloppy on, and it matters more than the schedule.

Thawing

  • In the refrigerator until fully thawed, the standard method. Or seal it in a bag and submerge it in cool to lukewarm water, changing the water as needed, until there is no frozen core left.
  • Never on a counter at room temperature for hours, and never in a microwave. A microwave heats unevenly, leaving a frozen center beside hot pockets that can burn the snake's mouth or make the prey burst.
  • Offer it at room temperature or a little warmer, never cold from the refrigerator and never hot. Warm it gently, for example by running warm water over the outside of the sealed bag, and check often by touch.
  • Offer it from feeding tongs, never your fingers. Most bites in this species are feeding mistakes, page 16.

Storage

  • Food held at a steady 0°F (−18°C) stays safe indefinitely, but quality declines the longer it sits. Keep prey sealed and airtight, and do not let stock sit for a year or more.
  • Thaw once. A thawed rodent is never refrozen. If the snake will not eat it, it is a loss, not leftovers.
Frozen rodents carry Salmonella too Several Salmonella outbreaks in people have been tied to frozen feeder rodents. Wash your hands with soap and water right after handling them or anything where they were stored or thawed. Keep them away from where human food is stored, made or eaten, use containers and utensils that never touch human food, never thaw prey in the kitchen sink you use for dishes, and never use a kitchen microwave or kitchen utensils on it.

Where to feed: a separate container

Hognoses are enthusiastic, somewhat messy eaters and are prone to swallowing substrate along with their food. Feed in a separate container, away from the loose substrate this species needs. It is the single most effective way to prevent impaction, and it is worth doing as standard practice rather than only after a problem.

StepHow
The containerA plain lidded plastic tub with air holes, lined with paper towel. Plain, lined, boring, easy to clean: the one place the setup should look nothing like the display enclosure
Moving the snake inLift it out of the substrate with a snake hook, never a bare hand that smells of mouse. Most bites happen with a hungry snake, or while it is being moved into a feeding container
Offering the preyFrom tongs, never fingers
Moving it backOnce it has swallowed, move it back gently and briefly, by hook or by letting it crawl, with no handling session. Then leave it alone for 48 hours

If the snake refuses, throw the prey out rather than saving it, since thawed prey is never refrozen, and work through the refusal checklist that follows.

Beastly FactsHognose Snake Care Package · Edition 1.112
Section 03 · Feeding

The refusing hognose

This species has a reputation for turning down food. A refusal is usually a puzzle, not an emergency.

A hatchling that turns down a meal is not automatically in trouble, and neither is an adult that skips a few. Work through the causes in order: first the enclosure, then the season and the snake's own cycle, then the prey itself. A refusal becomes a vet question when it comes with weight loss or any other sign of illness. A hatchling or juvenile has far less in reserve than an adult, so weigh a young snake every week through any refusal and call the vet sooner.

Causes and what to do

CauseHow you can tellDo
Enclosure too coolRead the thermometers; check the probeFix the gradient on page 7 before anything else
New arrivalHome for less than two weeksLeave it alone to settle, then try again
A shed comingColors fade, eyes cloudy blue, hides more, more defensiveOffer again after the shed. Page 29
Breeding seasonAn adult male ready to breed may refuseNot fixed by offering more food. Weigh it and wait
Seasonal slowdownLate fall or winter; prefers the cool end, may stay buried for weeksNormal while its weight holds. Page 21
After a regurgitationA meal brought back up in the last two weeksNo food for two weeks, then a small meal. Page 27
Picky about plain miceA healthy, settled hatchling ignores a plain pinkyScent the prey, below

Scenting

One practical threshold: start scenting if a snake refuses its first three meal offerings. Scent the thawed prey with one of these:

  • Fish: sardine, tuna or salmon.
  • Chicken bone broth.
  • Frog, toad, lizard or gecko scent, or commercial scent strips, the packaged option. The amphibian scents work because they match what the species evolved eating.

Change one thing at a time and keep the feeding record, so you know what worked.

When a refusal becomes a vet visit Weight down more than 10% from the snake's starting weight, or visibly thinner along the spine and tail base. Wheezing, open-mouth breathing, or bubbles or discharge at the nose or mouth. Excess saliva, tiny red spots on the gums, or cheesy yellow material in the mouth. Lethargy well beyond the season's usual quiet. Still refusing by spring, or refusing out of season while losing weight. Any of these ends the wait.
Refused or regurgitated? A refused meal is a snake that never struck. A regurgitated meal was eaten and came back up. The first usually needs patience. The second means something in the setup, the handling or the snake's health is wrong, and it has its own plan.
Beastly FactsHognose Snake Care Package · Edition 1.113
Section 04 · Handling & Behavior

Handling & hygiene

Short, calm, supported sessions, never near a meal, and soap and water every time.

Give a new hognose about two weeks to settle before the first session. After that:

  1. Signal that this is not food. Lift the snake out of the substrate with a small tool such as a snake hook, then move it onto your hands.
  2. Come in from the side. A hand or tool dropping from above looks like a predator and sets off the hood and hiss.
  3. Support as much of the body as you can. Let it rest along your palms and forearm. Never grab the tail and never restrain the head.
  4. Let it move. Keep your hands under it as it crawls, moving one hand ahead of the other.

How long and how often

RuleDetail
First sessionsNo more than 5 minutes, and end on a calm snake, not mid-display
Building upTo 10 minutes, then to as much as half an hour. Never past an hour
How oftenOnce or twice a week is plenty, and never more than once a day
Skip a session whenIt has eaten in the last 48 hours; it is in a shed (eyes cloudy or blue); it is mid-dig

Salmonella and the household

Every reptile can carry Salmonella, bacteria that live in the gut of a perfectly healthy snake with no sign of illness and leave in its droppings. A single negative test is not a clean bill of health, so treat every reptile as a carrier. The risk is not the bite. It is hands and surfaces to mouth: the snake, its water, its substrate and its gear all carry it.

  • Wash your hands with soap and running water right after touching the snake, the enclosure, the water or anything that has touched them.
  • Keep the snake and its gear out of the kitchen, and never clean the enclosure, dish or tools in a kitchen sink, a bathroom sink or a bathtub people use. A dedicated tub or bin solves this.
  • Don't kiss the snake or hold it close to your face.
  • Children under 5 should not handle reptiles or touch their enclosures at all. Adults over 65, pregnant people and anyone with a weakened immune system are also at higher risk of serious illness.
If someone in the house gets sick Diarrhea, fever and stomach cramps are the ordinary symptoms, which is why the link to a pet gets missed. Mention the snake to the doctor even if nobody remembers touching it, especially for anyone in a higher-risk group.
Beastly FactsHognose Snake Care Package · Edition 1.114
Section 04 · Handling & Behavior

Hooding, hissing & playing dead

One of the most dramatic defensive acts of any pet snake, and almost all of it is bluff.

When a hognose feels threatened it puts on a show, usually in this order. It inflates its body with deep breaths and flattens its neck into a cobra-like hood, the source of its "puff adder" nickname. It hisses loudly. It throws closed-mouth mock strikes that never make contact. If none of that works, some hognoses go further and play dead: they roll onto the back, writhe, open the mouth and let the tongue hang out, and sometimes release musk, a foul-smelling fluid, or feces. Flip one back over mid-performance and it will often roll itself belly-up again, as if it has not noticed. Playing dead is called death feigning, or thanatosis.

What it means A hognose putting on the full display is doing everything it can to avoid biting you. Real aggression in this species is close to unheard of. The act is hardwired, not illness and not a personality, and it is not a sign the snake is about to bite. Bites come from a different place entirely: food.

What the research adds

A field study of 27 wild western hognoses, published in the journal Ethology by Durso and Mullin, simulated predator attacks and timed the response. Larger snakes played dead for longer than smaller ones, and that link was stronger in females than in males. Snakes found at higher temperatures started playing dead sooner. For a keeper, that means a big female may hold the act a long time, and that is still normal.

What to do when it happens

  • Stay calm and keep your hands steady. Panicking and dropping the snake is the classic first-timer mistake. Calm, steady handling works better.
  • If it rolls over, stop. Put it down somewhere safe, step back, and let it right itself on its own. Do not keep flipping it.
  • Approach from the side next time. A hand or tool dropping from above looks like a predator and sets off the act. Page 14.

Normal, or worth a look

NormalWorth a look
Hooding and hissing when startled or disturbed, then settlingHooding and hissing at every routine interaction, for weeks. A snake doing this constantly is reporting something about its enclosure: more cover and deeper substrate at both ends usually reduce it.
Rolling over and lying limp, then righting itself once left alone in a quiet roomLimp or unresponsive with no trigger, or still limp long after it has been left alone at normal temperature. That is not the act: call a vet the same day
More defensive in the days before a shedA snake that stays defensive and stops eating outside a shed. Check the setup first
Beastly FactsHognose Snake Care Package · Edition 1.115
Section 04 · Handling & Behavior

The venom question & bites

Mildly venomous, not dangerous, and worth respecting at feeding time.

The western hognose is rear-fanged and mildly venomous. It has enlarged, ungrooved fangs toward the back of the upper jaw, connected to a gland in front of them called the Duvernoy's gland, which produces a weak venom evolved to help it subdue toads. Bites are uncommon and their effects stay local, though a snake that holds on can cause real swelling and bruising. A 2026 study calls it the most commonly kept venomous pet snake in the world.

What the research says

StudyWhat it found
Weinstein and Keyler, 2009, a case report in the journal ToxiconA keeper was bitten while offering a young mouse to a captive snake, which held on to the inside of the elbow for several minutes. The result was marked local swelling, bruising, swollen lymph nodes (the small glands that fight infection), skin signs of a mild cellulitis (an inflamed skin infection) and blisters. There were no effects anywhere else in the body, and recovery was complete after about five months. The authors concluded that hognoses may uncommonly produce medically significant bites but should not be considered dangerous, and that captive snakes should be handled carefully, particularly when offered food
Damm and colleagues, 2026, a survey of keepers in Frontiers in Amphibian and Reptile Science63 bite reports, 34 of them with symptoms. 24 of the 63 happened during feeding, and most involved a hungry snake or one being moved into a feeding container. Quick strike-and-release bites caused no symptoms 37% of the time (14 of 38), and the rest cleared within 2 days. Bites where the snake held on or chewed produced symptoms 80% of the time, lasting on average 3 days for a hold and 6 for a chew. Local swelling was by far the most common symptom. 7 of the 63 sought medical help. The authors judged the species relatively harmless, unable to cause permanent damage or death, and in need of no legal regulation for its venom

How bites happen, and how to avoid them

Real bites are rare and are almost always a feeding response: the snake mistakes a hand for food. So: wash prey scent off your hands before handling; lift the snake out with a snake hook rather than a bare hand, especially on feeding day; offer food from tongs; and leave it alone for 48 hours after a meal. The survey's authors add that proper equipment, leather gloves or a snake hook, and getting the snake off quickly would prevent virtually all envenoming, the term for venom actually entering the body.

If a bite happens and the snake hangs on Get it off quickly, because the longer a hognose holds and chews, the more symptoms follow. But do not yank it off, which can injure both of you. Pour cool water over its face and it will usually let go on its own. Then show a doctor any bite that breaks the skin: tell them it was a rear-fanged hognose. Rare allergic reactions are possible, as with any bite, so get emergency care for any reaction beyond the bite site itself.

None of this puts the western hognose in the category state venomous-reptile laws are written for: several of those laws exempt hognoses by name. The one place the venom does decide the answer is New York City. Pages 22 to 24.

Beastly FactsHognose Snake Care Package · Edition 1.116
Section 04 · Handling & Behavior

Enrichment & common mistakes

Researchers let western hognoses choose. They chose enrichment, and chose it more strongly as time went on.

Nagabaskaran, Skinner and Miller ran a preference test, published in the journal Animals in 2022. Each enclosure was divided in two. The enriched half had burrowing substrate, objects to interact with, and a large water dish. The standard half had paper towel and a small dish. Both halves had a shelter, and there was a heat gradient, so the test compared enrichment on top of adequate care, not enrichment against neglect. Over six days of observation:

  • The snakes preferred the enriched side, and the preference grew stronger over time, which rules out simple curiosity about something new.
  • The preference was stronger when the enriched side was the cooler one, which the authors link to this species' burrowing.
  • Boldness made no difference. A shy hognose is not opting out of enrichment.

Priority order

  1. Substrate deep enough to burrow into completely
  2. That deep substrate placed on the cool side
  3. A water dish large enough to soak in
  4. Secure cover at both ends of the gradient
  5. Scent novelty and varied feeding presentation
  6. Rearranging the furnishings, and new objects, last

Common mistakes

MistakeWhy it matters
Misting, or a damp enclosureThe root of respiratory infection and scale rot. Page 9
Paper towel as the permanent floorIt is the exact condition the study's standard side represented. Paper towel is right for quarantine, page 18, and not after
Deep substrate on the warm endIt pits two preferences against each other
Feeding on the substrateImpaction. Page 12
An adult on a hatchling's scheduleObesity and a shorter life. Page 11
A heat source with no thermostatBurns. Page 8
Reading the hood as personalityIt is a threat response. Page 15
Handling a snake that is mid-dig, or within 48 hours of a mealIt interrupts the behavior the enclosure exists for, and the second invites a feeding bite
Collecting a wild hognoseIllegal in many states, and an eastern or southern hognose is often protected. Page 22
Beastly FactsHognose Snake Care Package · Edition 1.117
Section 05 · Arrival & Life Stages

Choosing a hognose, quarantine & the first vet visit

Captive-bred, eating frozen-thawed mice, and kept apart for months. In that order.

Buy captive-bred. Compared with wild-caught animals, captive-bred reptiles are less likely to bite, more likely to accept the food offered, and less likely to carry parasites. A breeder who hatched the snake can tell you when it hatched, what it eats, and when it last ate and shed. A shop or breeder is worth buying from only if its enclosures are clean and large enough. A rescue snake often arrives with no reliable history, and an expo puts animals from many sellers in one room for a day. Neither is a reason to refuse the animal. Both are reasons to run the full quarantine below.

Look before you pay

CheckHealthyWalk away or ask more
EyesClear and alertSwollen, sunken, crusted, or cloudy outside a shed
Nose, breathingDry nostrils, quiet breathingBubbles, mucus, wheezing, open-mouth breathing
Vent (the rear opening under the tail)CleanStained, pasted with feces, or swollen
BodyRounded, no ridge of spine showingVisible bones, or well behind its age in size
Skin and shedIntact, no old shed left onWounds, or rings of old shed on the tail tip
MitesNone visibleTiny black, brown, red or orange specks, especially around the eyes
BehaviorTongue flicking, aware, good muscle toneLimp or unresponsive. A hood and a hiss at a stranger's hand is normal, page 15

Ask the seller: the hatch date; whether it was captive-bred; what it eats, when it last ate, and whether it takes plain or scented frozen-thawed mice; whether it has been treated for anything, mites or a respiratory infection above all; and for a receipt naming Heterodon nasicus. A good breeder answers without looking anything up.

Quarantine: 3 to 6 months

Quarantine means keeping a new animal completely apart from any other reptile. A new reptile needs 3 to 6 months of it. If this is your only reptile, the separation rules below have nothing to protect, but the first vet visit and its fecal test still apply.

RuleHow
A separate roomA second enclosure on the same shelf shares the same air. A different room is the real separation
Paper towel floorIt shows mites, stool and regurgitated food at a glance. Just a hide and a water dish, things you can disinfect or throw out
Separate toolsTongs, dish, scoop, even the paper towel roll
New animal lastCare for established animals first, every time. Wash your hands, or change gloves, between
Restart the clockIf anything flags, a positive fecal test, a regurgitation, unexplained weight loss, start the window again
Find the vet before the snake comes home Not every practice treats reptiles. The Association of Reptile and Amphibian Veterinarians runs a find-a-vet directory. Ask a clinic how many reptiles it sees, whether it treats snakes routinely, whether it runs fecal tests (stool checks for parasites) in house, and who covers emergencies after hours. Book the first exam within 72 hours of bringing the snake home, and no later than two weeks, with a fresh stool sample in a sealed bag. That visit records a baseline weight and the snake healthy.
Beastly FactsHognose Snake Care Package · Edition 1.118
Section 05 · Arrival & Life Stages

Telling the sex, weight & body condition

Sex is a vet's job. Weight and body condition are yours, every week.

Telling male from female

Snakes show no outside sign of sex that an owner can trust. Two hands-on methods work, and both are procedures with real technique behind them:

MethodHow it worksWho should do it
ProbingA lubricated, blunt metal probe slides into the vent and back along the tail. In a male it goes deeper, into the pocket holding a hemipenis (one of a male snake's paired reproductive organs), about 6 to 14 scales; in a female it stops at about 3 to 6A reptile vet or experienced breeder only. The wrong size or angle injures the snake
PoppingGentle pressure at the base of a hatchling's tail turns the hemipenes outward in a maleA reptile vet or experienced breeder only. Too much force injures the tail
UltrasoundImaging that shows the internal organs. Reliable in snakes and needs no handling of the ventA reptile vet

Tail shape is a weak guess on one animal with nothing to compare it against. In an adult hognose, size is a strong hint, because females run so much larger, but it is a hint, not confirmation.

Weigh it every week

Weight, not length, is the number that tells you how a snake is doing. Weigh it once a week on a kitchen scale in grams: set a lidded tub on the scale, zero it, then add the snake. One reading tells you little. Three or four in a row, climbing, holding or falling, tell you a great deal, and it is the direction of that line that should drive a feeding change or a vet call. Use page 5 for rough adult weights, and your own snake's record for everything else.

The weight line to watch A drop of more than 10% from the snake's normal weight, or a steady fall across several weeks, is a vet visit, whatever the season. A sudden drop is the first thing to show the vet.

Body condition: the cross-section test

Support the snake and look at it end-on, picturing a slice straight across its body.

ShapeWhat you see and feelDo
RightA rounded loaf, full and even, no sharp angles. Muscle over bone along the backKeep going
Too thinTriangular, sloping away from a ridge down the middle of the back where the spine sits close to the surfaceOver several checks, and with falling weight, a vet visit: thinness is as often parasites or illness as underfeeding
Too heavyRound in a different way: skin folds along the sides, or a soft, doughy feel over the ribsFeed smaller or less often, page 11. Do not stop feeding outright

The 9-point body condition scale used for dogs and cats does not apply to a snake's body. The cross-section check is the one that fits, and it is the one a reptile vet uses.

Beastly FactsHognose Snake Care Package · Edition 1.119
Section 05 · Arrival & Life Stages

Females, eggs & eggs that get stuck

For anyone keeping a female that has been with a male, or bought from a breeder who paired her.

This page is not a breeding guide. It is what a keeper of a female needs to recognize, so that a normal clutch is handled calmly and a stuck one gets to a vet in time. A female is gravid when she is carrying eggs.

What a normal clutch looks like

StageWhat happens
MatingIn the wild, June to August. Wait until a female is at least 2 years old, preferably closer to 3, and 150 to 200 g
The pre-lay shedShe sheds, then lays on average 7 to 11 days later. That shed is your signal to put the laying box in
The clutch4 to 23 eggs in a wild female, around 13 on average. Captive clutches have topped 30
Hatching52 to 64 days in the wild. In an incubator at 78 to 82°F (25.6 to 27.8°C), 51 to 60 days

The laying box

A plastic food container with a hole cut in the lid, filled about halfway with loamy soil. Put it in after the pre-lay shed and leave her alone. Solitude and a suitable place to lay are what she needs, and an inadequate nest site is one of the causes of eggs getting stuck.

Egg binding

Egg binding, also called dystocia, is when a female cannot pass her eggs. It is life-threatening.

Egg binding
CausePoor husbandry, an inadequate nest site, an inappropriate diet, and dehydration
SignsA female past her expected laying window who becomes lethargic, weak or unresponsive. It is not usually sudden: reptiles can hold eggs for weeks or even months, so a female that has not laid when expected needs watching closely
DiagnosisThe vet examines her and uses X-ray images and ultrasound to find the eggs
ResponseImmediate vet evaluation. The vet may try medical treatment and better conditions, but medical management often fails and surgery is needed in most cases. Never give any medication at home: the vet chooses the treatment and sets any dose
RecoveryDepends on how long the eggs were held and what the surgery involved. She rests, and the vet decides when feeding restarts
A female kept alone Whether a female hognose kept on her own will produce eggs is not well documented. If your adult female swells, sheds and then turns restless or stops eating with no male in the picture, describe it to your vet rather than guessing.
Beastly FactsHognose Snake Care Package · Edition 1.120
Section 05 · Arrival & Life Stages

The winter slowdown

A hognose may go off food and stay buried for weeks in winter. The question is never the appetite alone.

In the wild a western hognose spends roughly September to March below ground. Brumation is the reptile version of that seasonal slowdown, tied to temperature and daylight: less activity, less appetite, a slower metabolism. It is not the same as a mammal's hibernation, and a brumating snake can still wake, move and drink.

A pet hognose kept at steady temperatures needs no deliberate brumation. That is a breeder's tool for bringing on reproduction. But a pet may slow down on its own in late fall even with nothing changed: less active, buried for weeks, off food, and preferring the cool end. That is fine while its weight holds. The trouble is that illness also starts with a refused meal, so check the rest of the snake.

CheckNormal seasonal slowdownIllness: call a reptile vet
TemperaturesUnchanged, verified at both endsA failed heater or thermostat explains the fast. Fix it first, then watch
Weight, every 1 to 2 weeksStable, or a slow drift well inside 10% of the starting weightDown more than 10%, or visibly thinner along the spine and tail base
BreathingQuiet, mouth closedOpen-mouth breathing, bubbles or discharge at the nose or mouth, wheezing
MouthPink, clean gumsExcess saliva, tiny red spots on the gums, cheesy yellow material
BehaviorHides more and prefers the cool end, but moves normally when handledLethargy well beyond the usual slowdown
TimingStarts in fall, ends by springStill refusing food by spring, or refusing out of season

A snake that passes every line can be left alone with fresh water available and weighed every one to two weeks. To weigh a snake that is buried, lift it gently and weigh it in a lidded tub.

Deliberate brumation is an advanced technique

Some keepers cool a western hognose on purpose: stopping food at the beginning of November so the gut empties, then about 3 months of cooling from December to the end of February. It is for an experienced keeper, usually breeding, and only for a healthy snake at a good weight with a clean bill of health from a reptile vet, since cooling an underweight or parasite-carrying snake adds real risk. Lower and raise temperatures gradually over a week or two, keep water available throughout, and offer the first meal only once the snake has been back at normal temperatures for several days and is active.

Stop and warm it back up if It loses more than 10% of its starting weight, shows any sign of respiratory illness (wheezing, mucus, open-mouth breathing), is lethargic well beyond the expected slowdown, or does not wake as expected. Then call the vet.
Beastly FactsHognose Snake Care Package · Edition 1.121
Section 06 · The Law

Is a hognose legal where you live?

Broadly legal. The exceptions turn on native-species law far more often than on venom, and on which hognose you have.

This section covers all 50 states, Washington, D.C. (the District of Columbia) and New York City, which has its own rules. Of those 52, a pet hognose is legal in 27, conditional in 15, permit-only in 4, and banned in 6. The note beside each says which hognose the rule reaches, because in several states that differs between the western and the eastern. Three of the six bans, Georgia, New York State and West Virginia, reach only their native hognoses, not the western.

LegalThe state's own rules allow a pet hognose with no permitPermitLegal, but a permit or license comes first
ConditionalLegal without a permit only if a stated condition is met, very often which species it isBannedCannot be kept as a pet, and no permit route exists
The venom question, legally The mild venom almost never decides the answer. Several state venomous-reptile laws name hognoses as an exception: Kentucky and Alabama write "except for hognose snakes (genus Heterodon)" into the rule itself. What catches hognoses is native-wildlife law. The eastern and southern hognoses are native and often protected, and a few states protect the western as their own native too. The one place the venom itself decides it is New York City.

Banned

WhereWhy
GeorgiaBoth Georgia hognoses, the eastern and the southern, are on the Department of Natural Resources list of native species that "may not be held as a pet regardless of its origin or morphology," so a captive-bred animal or a color form is caught too. The western is not a Georgia species and is not on that list, so which hognose you have decides it. Check with the department before keeping any hognose
HawaiiEvery snake is banned, with no exception for harmless species
KansasBoth Kansas hognoses, the western (named in the rule as the plains hog-nosed snake) and the eastern, are listed as nongame species in need of conservation, and no rule or permit allows keeping one. An animal held before the rule may be kept only if an affidavit was filed and approved before 1 January 1990
New York StateThe eastern hognose is a protected native snake with no open season and a species of special concern, and a captive-bred animal from another state is treated the same. The only possession license is not issued for pets. The western is not a New York species and the state rule reaches only the eastern, so which hognose decides it. Confirm with the Department of Environmental Conservation
New York CityThe city health code bans every venomous, rear-fanged colubrid (a member of the snake family Colubridae) with a Duvernoy's gland, "even if devenomized." That reaches the western hognose. A prohibited animal can be seized
West VirginiaThe state bars keeping any native reptile not on a short permitted list, which names no snake. The eastern hog-nosed snake is on the state's checklist of native snakes

Permit

WhereWhy
IllinoisThe western hognose is listed as a threatened species in Illinois, so keeping one needs a Department of Natural Resources threatened species possession permit, and breeding or selling one needs a separate propagation permit at $150 a year. The eastern is not listed and falls under the ordinary cap of 4 per species and 8 in total. Cities can be stricter
MissouriBoth the eastern and the western are Missouri natives and are not treated as venomous, which puts them in Class I of the state Wildlife Code. Confirm what that requires with the Department of Conservation
New JerseyBoth need a permit: the eastern as a native nongame species, the western as an exotic reptile. Taking an eastern from the wild is separately illegal, so a permitted one has to be captive-bred
New MexicoAll three hognoses are on the importation list in Group III, a permit with specific conditions attached. The rule covers bringing an animal into the state rather than keeping one already there
Beastly FactsHognose Snake Care Package · Edition 1.122
Section 06 · The Law

States with conditions

Fifteen states where a hognose is legal only on a stated condition. Read the condition, then check which species you have.
WhereThe condition
AlabamaOnly the southern hognose is protected, and keeping one needs a scientific collection permit or a written permit from the Commissioner. The eastern and the western are unrestricted, and the state's venomous-reptile ban names hognoses as an exception
ColoradoA captive-bred western hognose is allowed with documentation and no license, under the rule in effect from 1 May 2026. The eastern is excluded by name. A hognose taken from the wild in Colorado is lawful only if held on or before 1 May 2026 and reported by 30 July 2026; no new wild capture. Check your city or county too
ConnecticutThe eastern is a State Species of Special Concern and needs a permit to import or possess. The western is not a Connecticut species and is unrestricted
DelawareThe eastern is native and not available for private ownership, except a captive-bred animal in an unusual color form held under permit. The western, not a Delaware species, needs an Individual permit from the Department of Agriculture
IndianaThe eastern is an Indiana native: selling, offering or transporting one for sale is barred whatever its origin, and keeping is capped at 4 of a native species. Captive-bred albino, leucistic (pale) or xanthic (yellow) color forms are exempt, and a captive breeding license allows sales. The western is not on the list
MarylandThe eastern: one per person without a permit. The western is outside the rule and unrestricted. Counties can be stricter, so check the local rule first
MassachusettsThe western is exempt by name. The eastern is a state species of special concern, which puts it in a permit tier the state does not issue for pets, captive-bred or not
MichiganThe eastern is native and may be taken only with a fishing license, at limits of 3 a day and 6 in total across snakes, lizards and turtles, and reptiles may not be bought or sold. The western is not a Michigan species and is legal. Local rules can be stricter
MinnesotaA snake from a permitted breeder, or one held before 1 August 2021, may be kept as a pet. Both hognoses are Minnesota natives. The breeder permit system is not visibly in place yet, so ask the Department of Natural Resources how a buyer meets the condition
NebraskaBoth hognoses are capped at 3 per species for collected animals. One legally bought from outside Nebraska may be kept with no number limit, if you can show proof of legal purchase such as a bill of sale. Keep the receipt
OklahomaBoth hognoses reach Oklahoma. A hunting license is required to take or possess a land reptile, with a limit of 6 per species, and state law exempts a legally obtained pet from a source other than the wild from the possession ban. Ask the Department of Wildlife Conservation which applies to your snake
PennsylvaniaThe eastern is native, with no open season and a limit of zero, and cannot be imported. The western is outside the rule, so a captive-bred western from a shop is lawful
TexasBoth hognoses are on the state nongame list: up to 25 per species without a permit, and no selling, trading or bartering any of them. This applies to captive-bred animals too
VirginiaThe eastern is a Species of Greatest Conservation Need and may not be possessed for private use in any number. The western is a nonnative animal and needs no permit
WisconsinThe eastern is native, capped at 5 until the end of 2026. From 1 January 2027 only captive-bred color variants from a legal source may be kept, and a wild-type eastern already held must be registered with the Department of Natural Resources by 30 June 2027. The western is not a Wisconsin species
Beastly FactsHognose Snake Care Package · Edition 1.123
Section 06 · The Law

States where it is legal

Twenty-seven jurisdictions with no state permit for a pet hognose. A few still have a catch.
WhereNote
Maine, New Hampshire, Oregon, Rhode IslandEach names the western hognose specifically. The eastern is a different answer: in Maine it is a native left off the list; in New Hampshire it is controlled separately; in Oregon it is on no list and may not be possessed; in Rhode Island keeping one as a pet is prohibited. Oregon cities and counties can be stricter. Maine's list was last verified in August 2026
KentuckyThe venomous-snake ban lists the colubrid family and then carves hognoses straight back out by name. Local rules can be stricter
FloridaCleared as a nonvenomous, unprotected reptile. Neither Florida hognose is on the state's imperiled species list
California, Montana, North Carolina, Ohio, WashingtonLegal at state level, but cities and counties may prohibit what the state allows. Check your local ordinance (a city or county law). In Ohio the eastern is native, and collecting one is a wildlife agency question
NevadaCleared as a nonvenomous reptile not native to Nevada. Clark County, Las Vegas and Henderson are stricter than the state: check the city first
Arizona, WyomingLegal to keep a captive-bred animal. Hognoses live wild in both states, and taking one from the wild is a separate question with its own license and limits. The Mexican hognose reaches southeastern Arizona
South DakotaNo possession permit, but a free entry permit applies to bringing any nondomestic animal into the state
District of ColumbiaIts short list of allowed pets includes nonvenomous snakes, and the hognose reads as permitted under it
Alaska, Arkansas, Idaho, Iowa, Louisiana, Mississippi, North Dakota, South Carolina, Tennessee, Utah, VermontNo state rule restricts a captive-bred pet hognose

Before you buy, wherever you live

  • Know the species. Get Heterodon nasicus and "captive-bred" on the receipt. In most of the conditional states, that line is the condition.
  • Never collect a wild hognose. Wild collection is restricted or banned in many states that allow captive-bred pets, and the eastern and southern hognoses are protected in several.
  • Check local rules. A city or county ordinance can be stricter than the state, and no state list covers it.
  • Moving? Check the new state before you go. A legal pet in one state can be capped, permit-only or banned in the next.
  • Keep the paperwork: the receipt, any permit, and the breeder's details. Nebraska and Colorado both turn on proof of legal origin.
Not legal advice This section is a summary of state rules as of October 2026, drawn from each state's regulations and agency pages, last checked on 1 October 2026 for every jurisdiction except Maine. It is not legal advice. Rules change, sometimes on a fixed date, as Wisconsin's will on 1 January 2027. Before you buy, check with your state wildlife agency, and with your city or county.
Beastly FactsHognose Snake Care Package · Edition 1.124
Section 07 · Health & Common Issues

Health red flags & finding a vet

Western hognoses are hardy. Most of what goes wrong traces back to humidity, substrate or feeding, all within your control.

Contact a reptile vet promptly if you see Open-mouth breathing, wheezing, drooling or mucus · no droppings with bloating and lethargy · belly scales discolored or blistered and getting worse · red spots on the gums, excess saliva or cheesy material in the mouth · mites · a burn · anything protruding from the vent · a meal brought back up twice · weight down more than 10% · limp or unresponsive at normal temperature · an eye cap still on after a shed · a female past her laying window who is weak or listless

What to tell the vet

Basking, cool-side and night temperatures, and what controls the heat
Humidity, and where you measured it
The last meal: date, prey, and whether it stayed down
When the signs started and whether they are getting worse
The last normal dropping, and what it looked like
The weight record from page 40, and a fresh stool sample in a sealed bag

Why the setup comes up first

Two of the most common problems in this species, respiratory infection and scale rot, share one cause: humidity or dampness running too high. Feeding on loose substrate causes impaction. Overfeeding against the snake's activity causes obesity. So a reptile vet will ask about your setup before anything else, and having the numbers ready shortens the visit. Snakes also hide illness well, which is why a weekly weight and a written record of meals, sheds and behavior catch problems before they show.

What a vet visit costs

Routine wellness exam$50 to $100
Fecal test (a stool check for parasites)$25 to $50
Radiograph, if needed$100 to $250 per view
Treating a respiratory infection, or an impactionCan run into the hundreds

Normal or concerning

NormalConcerning
Hooding, hissing or playing dead when disturbedLimp or unresponsive with no trigger. Page 15
Refusing a meal or two in good body condition, especially in winter or before a shedRefusal with weight loss, or with any other sign on this page. Page 13
Cloudy, blue eyes and faded color for a few days before a shedShed coming off in pieces, or an eye cap left on. Page 29
Buried for days at the cool end, weight steadyBuried and losing weight, or wheezing. Page 21
A semi-formed dropping with fur, and a white urateWatery or bloody droppings, or yellow or gritty urates. Page 30

Section 07 · Health & Common Issues

Respiratory & belly-scale infections

Two of the most common problems in this species, and the same root cause: too much moisture.

Respiratory infection

CauseHumidity running too high, temperatures too cool, or poor ventilation. This species prefers a dry setup, and dampness is more of a problem for it than for many other snakes. Unsanitary conditions, other illness and poor nutrition also contribute
SignsOpen-mouth breathing, wheezing, drooling or visible mucus, discharge from the nose, difficulty breathing, and lethargy
DiagnosisA reptile vet's examination, together with your temperature and humidity readings
ResponseAlways see a vet: it needs antibiotics and will not resolve on its own. The vet chooses the drug and sets the dose; never give leftover or bought antibiotics. At home, fix the cause at the same time: dry the enclosure, clean it, and hold the warm end correctly, because a sick snake is kept toward the upper end of its normal range. A respiratory infection gets worse in a snake kept too cool
RecoveryDepends on how early it is caught and on fixing the setup. If the humidity stays high, expect it to come back
The best tool for catching it early A digital thermometer and hygrometer, because they let you confirm the enclosure is running dry and warm rather than guessing. Page 9.

Scale rot (blister disease)

CauseDamp, dirty substrate
SignsDiscolored or blistered belly scales. Blister disease is the early stage of scale rot: the skin develops pustules (small pus-filled bumps) or blisters
DiagnosisA vet's examination of the skin
ResponseMove the snake to a clean, dry setup and keep the substrate dry and clean, which is what this species needs anyway. See a vet if it moves past mild discoloration; any treatment and dose are the vet's call
RecoveryCaught early, the blisters may heal without progressing to open sores. Left alone, they can
One cause, two diseases If you see either of these, read the hygrometer before anything else. A western hognose kept at 30 to 50% humidity, with no misting and a dry, clean bed, is very unlikely to see either one.
Beastly FactsHognose Snake Care Package · Edition 1.126
Section 07 · Health & Common Issues

Blockages, regurgitated meals & obesity

Three feeding problems, each with a feeding fix.

Impaction

Cause: a gut blocked by swallowed substrate. Hognoses are enthusiastic, somewhat messy eaters and are prone to swallowing substrate along with their food. Signs: a missed stool past its usual gap after a meal, then bloating, lethargy and refused food. The missed stool usually comes first. Diagnosis: a vet's examination, often with a radiograph. Response: there is no fixed number of days to wait, since the gap depends on meal size and temperature. A missed stool together with bloating, lethargy, refused food or regurgitation needs a reptile vet, not more waiting, and severe cases can need surgery. Prevention is feeding in a separate container, page 12. Recovery: depends on the blockage and how it was cleared; afterward, every meal goes in the feeding container.

Regurgitation

A hognose that brings up a meal undigested or half digested is telling you something went wrong around feeding. Cause: handling within 48 hours of a meal, an enclosure running too cool, stress, a meal that was too big, dehydration, a dirty enclosure, intestinal parasites, contaminated prey, or sharing the enclosure with another snake. Signs: the meal found in the enclosure or feeding tub. Diagnosis: working through that list, and a vet if it repeats, since repeated regurgitation after meals is also the main sign of Cryptosporidium (a stomach parasite, next page).

After a regurgitation Leave the snake completely alone: no handling and no feeding. Check the temperatures. After two weeks of steady improvement, offer a small meal, a quarter to half the usual size, then rest it again until the next feeding. A snake that looks worse after regurgitating, or brings up that small meal too, goes to a reptile vet.

Recovery: most snakes return to normal meals once the cause is fixed. The repeat is what matters, so log every one.

Obesity and fatty liver

Cause: in captivity a hognose gets less activity than in the wild and is sometimes fed too much or too often for its enclosure. The most common version is an adult kept on a hatchling's schedule. It is a real contributor to shortened lifespans in this species, and the serious end of it is fatty liver disease. Signs: a round cross-section with skin folds along the sides or a doughy feel over the ribs (page 19), and a weight that keeps climbing in an adult. Diagnosis: body condition and the weight record; a vet confirms and checks the liver. Response: match feeding frequency and portion to the adult's activity and size, page 11: smaller meals or longer gaps, not a sudden fast. Recovery: slow and steady over months, tracked on the scale.

Gout, the other cost of overfeeding Diets high in protein may predispose a reptile to uric acid building up, which can cause gout. Gout can be very painful, to the point that a reptile refuses to move, eat or drink. Yellow or gritty urates are an early hint. Diagnosis and any treatment are the vet's.
Beastly FactsHognose Snake Care Package · Edition 1.127
Section 07 · Health & Common Issues

Mites & internal parasites

Both are treatable, and both are why a new snake is quarantined. The third one here is not.

Snake mites

CauseTiny blood-feeding parasites, Ophionyssus natricis, most under 1.5 mm (millimeters) long. They spread by direct contact and shared equipment, almost always arriving on a new animal, used decor or tools
SignsTiny black, brown or red specks around the eyes, chin and vent, on the shed skin, or moving on the snake or the glass. Rubbing, lethargy, a lost appetite, coarse-looking skin, bad sheds, and long soaking in the water dish, as if trying to drown them
DiagnosisRub the snake gently over a sheet of white paper: mites that fall off show up against it. The vet confirms
ResponseA reptile vet treats the snake and sets the product, dose and schedule. You treat the enclosure the same week: clean it thoroughly, and throw away the substrate, branches and anything disposable. Use paper towel until the vet says it is clear
RecoveryGood when the snake and the enclosure are both treated. Treat only one and the mites come back. A heavy infestation causes anemia (blood loss) and can carry infections
Never treat a hognose for mites on your own Permethrin-based products (a common insecticide), pest strips and some over-the-counter mite sprays can be highly toxic to hognoses. Veterinary medicine does use a permethrin licensed for reptiles, which is exactly why the choice and the dose belong to the vet, not to a pet store shelf.

Internal parasites

Cause: worms and single-celled parasites, more common in wild-caught animals. Signs: weight loss despite eating, repeated watery droppings, regurgitation, or none at all. Diagnosis: a fecal test, which is why every new snake has one during quarantine and why periodic checks are worth it after. Response: a vet-prescribed antiparasitic drug at a dose the vet sets, plus a full enclosure clean. Recovery: usually good; the vet may retest to confirm.

Cryptosporidium

CauseCryptosporidium serpentis, a single-celled parasite of the stomach, and a serious concern in this species
SignsRegurgitation after meals, marked weight loss, slow decline, and often a firm swelling in the stomach region of the body that a vet can feel
DiagnosisA special stain of fresh droppings, or of the coating on a regurgitated meal
ResponseIsolate the snake and its tools, and see a vet. Several treatments have been tried and none has been especially effective
RecoveryThere is no reliable cure. That is the strongest argument on this page for buying captive-bred and running the full quarantine on page 18. The species found in reptiles is not thought to infect people
Beastly FactsHognose Snake Care Package · Edition 1.128
Section 07 · Health & Common Issues

Shedding, mouth infections, burns & tissue at the vent

One normal process to support, and three problems that each need a vet.

The shed cycle

Young hognoses shed most often. A shed is coming when the colors fade, the eyes turn cloudy blue, and the snake eats less, hides more and turns more defensive. The eyes stay cloudy for about 4 to 7 days, then clear, and the shed follows about 4 to 7 days after that. Leave it alone for that stretch: no handling and no rearranging. Shedding is called ecdysis.

Helping a dry-country snake shed Keep the rest of the enclosure dry and add moisture in one spot: mix water into the substrate in the humid hide to help a shed start or finish. Rough surfaces such as cork bark give it something to rub against. After the shed, find the skin and check that both eye caps and the tail tip came away with it.

Stuck shed, called dysecdysis, has six common causes: low humidity, skin parasites, nutritional problems, infectious disease, nothing rough to rub against, and low thyroid function. A shed that comes off in pieces now and then is not alarming; a pattern of bad sheds in a correct setup is a vet question. A retained eye cap (the clear scale over each eye, also called the spectacle) that extra moisture does not loosen needs a vet, and you never remove it yourself: left on, it can cause permanent eye damage and blindness.

Mouth rot (infectious stomatitis)

Cause: infection and inflammation of the tissue lining the mouth. Signs: tiny purplish-red spots in the mouth early, then excess saliva and cheesy yellow material along the teeth, and refused meals. Diagnosis: a vet's look inside the mouth. Response: a vet removes dead tissue, cleans with an antiseptic, and prescribes antibiotics and supportive care, at doses the vet sets. Recovery: best when treated early. A snake that is not eating because of it needs the vet's follow-up plan.

Burns

Cause: a snake resting on a spot that is too hot, or staying on a hot spot too long: an exposed lamp or bulb, a heat rock, an unregulated heat source, or a radiator or baseboard heater after an escape. Signs: damaged or discolored skin where the snake lay against the heat. Diagnosis and response: a vet, every time, plus the thermostat and screen fixes on page 8. Recovery: the vet judges it by how deep the burn goes.

Prolapse

Cause: tissue pushed out through the vent, the single rear opening, usually after straining: from impaction or constipation, dehydration, parasites, egg binding or bladder stones. The cloaca (the chamber just inside the vent), a male's hemipenes or part of the colon can be involved. Signs: moist tissue visible outside the vent. Response: an emergency. Keep the tissue clean and moist with a damp paper towel or clean cloth, do not push it back in, and get to a vet immediately: exposed tissue dries and swells fast. Diagnosis and recovery: the vet cleans and replaces the tissue and looks for the cause, because without fixing the cause it tends to come back.

Beastly FactsHognose Snake Care Package · Edition 1.129
Section 07 · Health & Common Issues

Reading droppings & hydration

The cheapest daily health check there is. Look before you scoop.

A snake does not pass liquid urine the way a mammal does. Its kidneys pull nitrogen waste out of the blood as uric acid, which leaves as urates: a white to cream, chalky or toothpaste-like paste. Because a snake has a single rear opening, the cloaca, the urates come out with the stool in the same pass. A snake generally does not pass a dropping until a meal is mostly digested, so the rhythm follows feeding: weekly for a weekly-fed juvenile, much less often for an adult fed every two weeks. Learn your own snake's normal; a real change from it is the signal.

It looks likeUsually meansDo
A semi-formed dropping with some fur or bone, and a smooth white urateNormal for a snake eating whole miceNothing. Note the date
Urate yellow, orange, or hard and grittyDehydration at least; if it persists, a urate or kidney problem, and the same chemistry as goutCheck the water dish is full and large enough to soak in, and the humid hide. Vet if it persists
Watery or unformed, more than once in a rowA classic sign of parasitic diseaseVet, with a fresh sample in a sealed bag. Page 28
Bright red bloodFresh bleeding near the ventVet the same day
Dark, tarryDigested blood from higher in the gutVet the same day
Straining, or visible discomfort passing wasteCan point to a blockage or a problem at the cloacaVet. Page 29 for prolapse
An unusually strong or off smellWorth a vet check alongside any other signNote it on the log
Nothing at all, with bloating and lethargyPossible impactionPage 27

Keeping a dry-country snake hydrated

Dry air does not mean a thirsty snake. A large water dish, emptied and refilled with fresh water every day, is the hydration plan, and the humid hide is the one damp spot in the enclosure. The urate is your fastest daily hydration read: smooth and creamy generally means a well-hydrated snake, and dry, hard or gritty is the signal to act. Dehydration is also on the list of causes of regurgitation, prolapse and egg binding, so it is worth getting right.

A soaking snake Soaking now and then, especially before a shed, is normal. A snake that suddenly will not leave its water dish is worth a close look at the eyes, chin and vent for mites.
