First 30 days

Most first-month problems come from doing too much: handling too soon, feeding too often, or fixing a hood and hiss that needs no fixing.

Before it arrives

Enclosure set up and running, heat, light and thermostat checked with both thermometers for a full day
Humidity confirmed 30 to 50%
Legal check done, and the receipt names Heterodon nasicus, captive-bred
Vet chosen; first exam booked within 72 hours
Asked the seller: hatch date, last meal, prey size, plain or scented

Week 1

Snake straight into its enclosure, or into quarantine if you keep other reptiles
No handling. Two weeks to settle
First vet exam with a fresh stool sample; record the baseline weight
Read both thermometers and the hygrometer daily
Fresh water daily; spot-clean droppings

Week 2

First feeding, in the feeding tub, on the seller's schedule and prey size
Leave it alone for 48 hours after
Refused? No panic. Page 13

Week 3

First handling session: lift out with a hook, from the side, no more than 5 minutes, end on a calm snake
Not within 48 hours of a meal, not during a shed
First weekly weigh-in in the log
Probe check: still where it belongs?

Week 4

Second weigh-in. Is the line flat, rising or falling?
Cross-section body condition check
Review the feeding record against page 11
Look over the droppings and urates, page 30

Throughout

Wash hands with soap after every contact; nothing cleaned in the kitchen sink
No misting, ever
Hooding, hissing, playing dead: step back and let it settle
Quarantine running its full 3 to 6 months, if you keep other reptiles
Sitter sheet, page 39, filled in before your first trip
The one thing to do every single day Read the thermometers and the hygrometer and write them down. A thermostat that has failed, a probe that has slipped, or a dish that has spilled into the substrate all show up in those numbers before they show up in the snake.

Section 09 · Owner Tools

Daily, weekly & seasonal routine

A low-maintenance snake, once the routine is written down.

Daily

Read both thermometers and the hygrometer
Read the second thermometer away from the thermostat probe
Empty, wash and refill the water dish
Pull droppings and urates as you see them; note what they looked like
Check lights came on and went off on time
Wash hands with soap after any contact

Weekly

Weigh in grams and write it down
Cross-section body condition check
Check the thermostat probe has not moved
Spot-check surfaces with the infrared thermometer
One or two short handling sessions, never within 48 hours of a meal

Every feeding

Thaw in the refrigerator; never the microwave or the kitchen sink
Feed in the tub, from tongs; record the date, prey and result
Wash hands, tongs and tub

Every shed

Moisten the humid hide substrate when the eyes cloud
Leave it alone until the shed is off
Check the skin for both eye caps and the tail tip

Every three months

Replace all substrate and disinfect, if the bed stayed dry and clean. Monthly if it went damp or smelly
Check the frozen mouse stock date

Yearly

Wellness exam and fecal test
Replace the UVB tube, if you use one, on the maker's schedule
Review prey size against current weight

Seasonal

Fall: expect a slowdown; weigh every 1 to 2 weeks while it lasts
Winter: watch night temperatures as the house cools; add heat with no light below 60°F (16°C)
Spring: appetite should return. Still refusing by spring is a vet visit
Summer: a hot room pushes the basking surface up; check it is not well above 95°F (35°C)

Section 09 · Owner Tools

Power outages, travel & transport

Heat is the one thing a snake cannot make for itself. For a hognose the line to hold is 60°F (16°C).

A healthy adult snake tolerates one ordinary cool night without harm. The risk is duration: sustained lower temperatures leave a reptile more open to infection and can stop it eating. For a hognose, room temperature is a normal night, and 60°F (16°C) is the point to add heat, move the snake, or call the sitter.

When the power goes out: do

  • Put a battery thermometer in the enclosure so you know the real number.
  • Drape thick towels or a blanket over it, leaving a vent gap.
  • Or move the snake in a ventilated tub to the warmest room, usually one without outside walls.
  • A wrapped hot water bottle or hand warmer beside the snake, never touching it.
  • Stop feeding until heat is reliably back. Keep water available.
  • More than a day or two below 60°F (16°C): board it with a vet or a friend with power.

Don't

  • Use candles, a gas stove or any open flame near the enclosure: a fire and carbon monoxide risk.
  • Put a heat pack against the snake. A cold, sluggish snake cannot move away in time.
  • Feed to "keep its strength up." Food sitting in a cold gut is a risk.
  • Warm a cold, unresponsive snake in hot water.

Call the vet if

Open-mouth breathing, wheezing or clicking, mucus at the nose or mouth, or a snake that stays limp once it is back at normal temperature.

Leaving town

TripAdultJuvenile, or a snake recovering from illness
1 to 2 nightsOften fine alone: lights on timers, thermostat running, fresh waterA sitter once a day for water and a temperature check
3 to 7 nightsA sitter every 1 to 2 days for water, droppings and a temperature check. Feed on the normal scheduleA sitter daily, with written instructions
Over a weekA daily sitter who has done a practice visit with you, or boarding with a reptile vet or reptile shop. Never a general dog and cat boarding facility

An adult fed every two weeks usually needs no feeding at all on a trip of a week. Time the meal before you leave, then let the sitter skip it.

Transport and vet trips

  • A ventilated plastic tub with a towel to grip, inside a dark bag or box. No loose substrate and no water dish.
  • Skip the meal before a trip. Warm the car first in cold weather, and on a trip over about 30 minutes below 65°F (18°C), add a wrapped hand warmer beside the tub.
  • Check it every 20 to 30 minutes at a stop. Never leave a snake in a parked car, hot or cold, even for a few minutes.
Outage kit, packed before you need it Two or three hand warmers or a hot water bottle, two thick towels, a battery thermometer, a ventilated tub, and the vet and emergency clinic numbers on paper, not only in a phone that might die.
Beastly FactsHognose Snake Care Package · Edition 1.138
Fill in and leave by the enclosure

Pet-sitter sheet

Empty, wash and refill the water dish

Normal readings

Basking surface90 to 95°F (32 to 35°C)
Cool side70 to 75°F (21 to 24°C)
NightRoom temperature, never below 60°F (16°C)
Humidity30 to 50%. Do not mist

Please don't

  • Pick the snake up unless we have discussed it. If it hoods, hisses or rolls over and plays dead, that is a normal bluff: step back and leave it.
  • Change any dial, timer or thermostat, mist the enclosure, or feed anything not on this sheet.
  • Handle frozen mice near human food, or thaw them in the microwave or kitchen sink.
Call me if The night reading is under 60°F (16°C) or the basking surface well over 95°F (35°C). The lights are off in the day. Open-mouth breathing, wheezing or mucus. Something sticking out of the vent. It is limp at normal temperature, or has not moved across two visits while out in the open. It has escaped. If I don't answer, call the vet number above.

Section 09 · Owner Tools

Owner log

One row a week. Photocopy this page, or track it digitally. Consistency matters more than the format.

DateWeight (g)Meal: prey, taken?Bask / cool °FHumidityDroppings, urateShedNotes
        
        
        
        
        
        
        
        
        
        
        
        
        
        
        
        

Weight: same scale, same tub, every week. Meal: write "R" for a refusal and "Reg" for a regurgitation. Shed: the date, and "eye caps off" once you have checked the skin.

Why bother logging A hognose that is getting sick often shows it on the scale before it shows it anywhere else. Sixteen rows is four months, long enough to see a real trend rather than a bad week, and it is the first thing a vet will want to see. For an adult, it is also how you notice the slow climb toward obesity.

Glossary, A to D

Albino, leucistic, xanthicBred color forms: albino lacks dark pigment, leucistic is pale overall, xanthic is yellow. Indiana exempts captive-bred animals in these forms. Page 23.
Ambient humidityThe humidity of the enclosure air in general, as opposed to inside the humid hide. 30 to 50% for this species. Page 9.
AnemiaToo few red blood cells, here from blood lost to mites. Page 28.
AntiparasiticA drug that kills parasites. The vet chooses it and sets the dose.
Basking surfaceThe flat spot under the heat lamp where the snake warms up: 90 to 95°F (32 to 35°C).
BioactiveA planted substrate with a cleanup crew of tiny invertebrates that break down waste.
BrumationThe reptile version of a winter slowdown: less activity, less appetite, slower metabolism. Not needed by a pet. Page 21.
Captive-bredHatched from parents kept by people, rather than caught in the wild. Several state laws turn on it.
CellulitisAn inflamed infection of the skin and the tissue under it. A sign in the 2009 bite case. Page 16.
Ceramic heat emitterA screw-in heater that gives off heat with no visible light, usable at night.
Cloaca and ventThe cloaca is the single chamber that waste, urates and eggs all pass through; the vent is its opening under the tail.
Color formA line bred for a color or pattern, also called a morph. The care is identical; only the price changes.
ColubridA member of the snake family Colubridae, the family the hognose is filed under in New York City's rule. Page 22.
ConditionalA legal status: allowed without a permit only if a stated condition is met. Page 23.
CryptosporidiumA single-celled stomach parasite of snakes with no reliable cure. Page 28.
D3Vitamin D3, the form of vitamin D a reptile's skin makes when UVB reaches it. Page 9.
Death feigningPlaying dead: rolling belly up, mouth open, tongue out. Also called thanatosis. Normal. Page 15.
DevenomizedVenom glands removed or disabled. New York City bans a hognose even if it has been. Page 22.
Dimming thermostatA thermostat that turns a heat lamp's power up and down like a light dimmer. The match for a halogen. Page 8.
Duvernoy's glandThe gland in the upper jaw that produces a hognose's mild venom, feeding the rear fangs. Page 16.
DysecdysisA bad or stuck shed. Page 29.
DystociaEgg binding: a female unable to pass her eggs. An emergency. Page 20.
Beastly FactsHognose Snake Care Package · Edition 1.142
Reference

Glossary, E to N

EcdysisShedding the skin. Page 29.
EnrichmentFeatures that let an animal do what it naturally does: for a hognose, above all, digging. Page 17.
EnvenomingVenom actually entering the body in a bite. Page 16.
Eye capThe clear scale over each eye, also called the spectacle. It sheds with the skin; one left on needs a vet.
Fecal testA lab check of a stool sample for parasites. Part of every new snake's first vet visit.
Ferguson zoneA ranking of reptiles by how much ultraviolet light they seek in the wild, zone 1 to zone 4. Hognoses are zone 2. Page 9.
Frozen-thawedPrey bought frozen and thawed before feeding. The standard for this species. Page 12.
Fuzzy, peach fuzzyA fuzzy is a young mouse with its first fur; a peach fuzzy sits between a pinky and a fuzzy. Page 11.
GoutA painful disease from uric acid building up in the joints or organs. High-protein feeding and dehydration push toward it.
GradientThe spread of temperatures from the warm end to the cool end, so the snake can choose. Page 7.
GravidCarrying eggs. Page 20.
Halogen basking bulbA bright, focused bulb that heats the spot beneath it. The usual day heat for this species.
HemipenesA male snake's paired reproductive organs, kept inside the base of the tail. What probing and popping detect.
HideA box, cave or piece of cork bark the snake can get fully inside, out of sight. Page 6.
HoodingFlattening the neck into a cobra-like hood as a bluff. Page 15.
HopperA young, weaned mouse, bigger than a fuzzy.
Humid hideA hide with moistened substrate or moss inside, the one damp spot in a dry enclosure. Page 9.
HygrometerA humidity meter. Digital, read at snake level.
ImpactionA gut blocked by swallowed substrate or other material. Page 27.
IncubationKeeping eggs warm until they hatch. Page 20.
Infrared thermometerA handheld point-and-read thermometer for surface temperatures.
Lymph nodesSmall glands that help fight infection; they swelled in the 2009 bite case.
MitesTiny blood-feeding parasites, Ophionyssus natricis in snakes. Page 28.
MuskA foul-smelling fluid released from the vent in defense.
Native speciesA species that lives wild in that state. Native-wildlife law is what restricts hognoses most often.
Nongame speciesWildlife that is not hunted for sport or food. Several states cap or protect native nongame reptiles.
Beastly FactsHognose Snake Care Package · Edition 1.143
Reference

Glossary, O to Z

OrdinanceA city or county law. It can be stricter than the state.
PermethrinAn insecticide. Some permethrin products are highly toxic to hognoses: mite treatment is the vet's call.
PinkyA newborn, hairless mouse, the first food for a hatchling.
Probing and poppingThe two hands-on ways to sex a snake. Vet or experienced breeder only. Page 19.
ProlapseTissue pushed out through the vent. An emergency. Page 29.
Pulse proportional thermostatA thermostat that sends short pulses of power. The match for a ceramic heat emitter.
PVCPolyvinyl chloride, the rigid plastic many enclosures are made of.
QuarantineKeeping a new animal apart from other reptiles for 3 to 6 months. Page 18.
RadiographAn X-ray image.
Rear-fangedWith enlarged fangs toward the back of the upper jaw rather than at the front.
RegurgitationA swallowed meal brought back up. Page 27.
Rostral scaleThe scale at the tip of the snout, upturned and shovel-shaped in a hognose for digging.
SalmonellaBacteria healthy reptiles carry and shed in droppings. Hands and surfaces to mouth is the risk. Page 14.
Scale rotA belly-skin infection from damp, dirty substrate; blister disease is its early stage, with pustules (small pus-filled bumps). Page 26.
ScentingRubbing prey with a scent such as fish or toad to tempt a refusing snake. Page 13.
Species of special concern, of greatest conservation needState conservation listings below threatened. Several states bar keeping the eastern hognose because of them.
StomatitisMouth rot: infection of the tissue lining the mouth. Page 29.
SubstrateThe loose material on the enclosure floor. Page 10.
T5 HOA slim fluorescent tube 5/8 in across (T5) in the high-output (HO) format. The usual UVB source.
ThermostatA controller that cuts the heat at a set temperature. Non-negotiable. Page 8.
UltrasoundImaging with sound waves. A non-invasive way for a vet to sex a snake or find eggs.
Unitsin, inches; ft, feet; cm, centimeters; mm, millimeters; g, grams; °F and °C, degrees Fahrenheit and Celsius; %, percent.
UratesThe white, chalky paste of uric acid passed with a reptile's droppings. Page 30.
UVBUltraviolet B, the part of sunlight a reptile's skin uses to make vitamin D3. Page 9.
UVIUltraviolet index, a measure of UVB strength at one spot. 1.1 to 3.0 where a hognose basks.
Wild-typeThe natural color and pattern, not a bred color form. The cheapest hognose to buy.

Sources

Where the numbers in this package come from, so you can check them yourself.

Beastly Facts guides drawn on

The hognose snake enclosure setup, feeding, health issues, handling, enrichment, cost and legal guides, and the hognose encyclopedia entry, carry every core husbandry figure: enclosure sizes by sex and age, temperatures, humidity, substrate, prey sizes and schedules, the refusal plan, the regurgitation plan, the display, the venom summary, the handling rules, setup and running costs and lifespan. The shared reptile guides carry the rest: quarantine and choosing a healthy reptile, heating and thermostats, the emergency plan with its hognose temperature row, snake sexing and body condition, snake brumation, shedding, Salmonella and hygiene with the cleaning schedule, reading stool and urates, and UVB lighting. The ball python feeding and health guides supply the thawing and storage method and the prolapse first aid, which do not depend on the species. The legal section comes from the Beastly Facts state legal research, checked 1 October 2026.

Research on this species

  • Weinstein and Keyler (2009), Toxicon 54(3): Local envenoming by the Western hognose snake (Heterodon nasicus): a case report and review of medically significant Heterodon bites. The bite case, its five-month recovery, and the conclusion that hognoses should not be considered dangerous.
  • Damm, Vilcinskas, Kreuels and Lüddecke (2026), Frontiers in Amphibian and Reptile Science: 34 reports of snakebite envenoming by the Western Hognose snake, a retrospective online survey. Bite counts, feeding context, hold time against symptoms, recovery times and the keeper recommendations.
  • Durso and Mullin, Ethology 120: Intrinsic and extrinsic factors influence expression of defensive behavior in Plains Hog-nosed Snakes. Death feigning by size, sex and temperature.
  • Nagabaskaran, Skinner and Miller (2022), Animals 12(23): Western hognose snakes prefer environmental enrichment. The preference study.
  • Kerns, Animal Diversity Web, University of Michigan: Heterodon nasicus. Range, habitat, length and weight, wild lifespan, toads in the diet, clutch size and hatching time, the winter season, and the state listings.
  • Galewood, Reptiles Magazine: Western Hognose Snake Care and Breeding. Adult lengths and weights by sex, hatchling weights, the pre-lay shed and laying box, incubation, and the warnings on permethrin and Cryptosporidium.
  • Healey, ReptiFiles: the hognose snake care guide and its pages on temperatures, humidity and lighting, handling and body language, brumation, and mites. The middle temperature band and 60°F (16°C) night floor, the basking stone, the UVB specification, cool water for a bite that holds on, and the brumation schedule.

Veterinary references

  • Merck Veterinary Manual, pet owner version: Disorders and Diseases of Reptiles. Respiratory infection, mouth rot, mites and the enclosure clean, blister disease, gout, prolapse, and egg binding diagnosis and treatment.
  • Merck Veterinary Manual: Parasitic Diseases of Reptiles. Cryptosporidium signs, diagnosis and treatment, the permethrin licensed for reptiles, and the role of quarantine.
  • Divers (1996), Proceedings of the Association of Reptilian and Amphibian Veterinarians: constipation in snakes. The missed stool that comes before a snake stops eating.
  • Zoo Med Laboratories: the ReptiSun 5.0 and 10.0 UVB T5 HO product pages. Tube lengths and wattages.
  • Spyder Robotics, Herpstat thermostat manual: probe placement, and the warning against aluminum tape on the probe.
  • VCA Animal Hospitals (originally Veterinary Centers of America): Common Snake Health Issues. Egg binding causes and signs, retained eye caps, burns and their causes, and the causes of a lost appetite.

The Beastly Facts guides cite further veterinary sources of their own, among them the Merck Veterinary Manual's reptile husbandry, nutrition and quarantine pages, VCA's snake housing page, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention on reptiles, amphibians and frozen feeder rodents, and Iowa State University's biosecurity guidance.

Where the sources disagree

Where credible sources give different numbers, this package prints one and says why.

TopicWhat the sources sayWhat this package uses
Night temperatureRoom temperature, no colder than 60°F (16°C), with no night heat needed (a specialist care sheet and the setup guide); a snake needs no night heat if the room holds 65 to 70°F (18 to 21°C) (the shared heating guide)Room temperature, adding heat with no light below 60°F (16°C)
Adult lengthMales 16 to 24 in, females 21 to 30 in (a breeder); 14 to 37 in, about 20 in average (a university account); 14 to 46 in for the genus; 1.5 to 3.5 ft for all hognoses; 2 to 3.5 ftThe breeder's split by sex, because enclosure size depends on it
Lifespan10 to 15 years commonly, 15 to 20 reported in captivity; 10 to 15 with one known 18-year-old; about 14 in the wild10 to 15 years, 15 to 20 reported
ActivityActive by day, most of all morning and late afternoon; or most active at dawn and duskActive by day, so a 12-hour light cycle
Quarantine3 to 6 months (veterinary); 60 to 90 days (hobby floor); 2 to 3 months (a care sheet)3 to 6 months
Mite treatmentA care sheet describes a home treatment with a diluted human lice product; a breeder warns permethrin products are highly toxic to hognoses; veterinary medicine uses a permethrin licensed for reptilesVet-only treatment, never a store product on your own
WeighingWeekly (the hognose health guide and a care sheet); monthly for a growing juvenile (the shared body condition guide)Weekly
Heat sourceA halogen over the substrate on a dimming thermostat (the setup and cost guides)Halogen by day; a mat or emitter only if the room drops below 60°F (16°C) at night
A bite that holds onRemove the snake quickly (a bite survey); do not pull it off, pour cool water on its face (the handling guide, a care sheet)Both: quickly, with cool water, never by yanking
UVB tube lifeEvery 12 months (a care sheet); 6 to 12 months by model (the UVB guide)The maker's schedule, no longer than 12 months
CostsSetup $200 to $500 (a common headline figure); priced line by line with every tool this package uses, $390 to $850, and $235 to $390 a year (the cost guide)Itemized: $390 to $850 of equipment, $235 to $390 a year (about $15 to $35 a month)
